doc.title: Rusty Dedrick interviewed by Monk Rowe, Ellenville, New York, June 23, 1998

title: Sideman pay, the union card and leaving Thornhill
summary: Prewar salaries, Norvo's pay games, the 802 card wait, and leaving Thornhill for his family.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: In fact I was going to ask you what the average salary of a sideman was in those years.

With Red it was like a low figure and you were lucky to get it. And not that he — it was a financial problem that he could not cope with. That was an old trick, and I should not take too much time on it, but if you worked a week here and then had two days off, they’d change the payday to conform to the next — Now after, with Claude, he had more backing and everything and that was not it. But the salary pre-war I would say ran like $150, something like that a week. Like we had Irving Fazola and Nick Fatool and later Irv —

Right. Thank you. And they were great players working for — You know at one point Billy Butterfield was getting his 802 card, so was Conrad Gozzo and I. And Billy came in and played third trumpet while he was getting his 802 card. And in doing an interview on WKCR they looked at the personnel on different record dates, and he said, “Are you sure that was the trumpet section?” It was.
Yeah the union was very strong wasn’t it.
What was the minimum age you had to be?

It wasn’t a matter of age, at least for me, I had to wait six months to get my card. I left Claude because I was married and my wife was pregnant and I didn’t want to travel anymore. I stayed in New York.
